newsitem.title: TURKEY: Political worries may cap uptrend in Turk stocks.
newsitem.headline: Political worries may cap uptrend in Turk stocks.

text.p: The Turkish stock market index hit its third consecutive all-time high this week on Friday but brokers say the uptrend might be capped by political concerns.

"With the opening of parliament, there is a growing feeling that the market is to be overshadowed gradually by politics. This might be the underlying issue for the stock market in coming days," said Ali Guler, chief analyst at Acar securities.
The stock market's IMKB-100 index rose by 1.9 percent to 76,694.86 percent on Friday.
It has gained nearly 20 percent since mid-September.
Murat Aktas of Tutunbank cited foreign investors' buying as the main reason for the rise.

Among the other factors behind the rise were expectations for good nine-month financial results and speculation that Turkey will introduce some tax incentives for those who keep stocks in their portfolios, and urge banks to keep one percent of their assets in stocks, he said.

Brokers say there is almost no fundamental reason to justify the recent uptrend. They believe the increased optimism that Turkey would reach an accord with the International Monetary Fund for a stand-by arrangement, and that rating agencies would not downgrade the country's rating helped stock prices rise.
Stock prices had remained cheap between July 8 and September 13 due to political concerns over the fate Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's coalition government.
The index was trapped in a range of 63,000 to 67,000 in the period and trade volume dropped to a daily average of around five trillion lira. It now runs at around 20 trillion lira.
Some analysts predict the index might test the 80,000 level in October. They said the market was encouraged by the satisfactory amount of a recent cash inflow.
"The surplus from the increased cash supply came into the stock exchange to take benefit of cheap prices and sparked the recent rise," Mustafa Oral, portfolio manager at Universal securities said.
However he said the inflow may turn to an outflow anytime.
"The money which flowed in is here only for short-term. It is ready to go back to bonds or currency in case of a negativity," Oral said.

A London-based foreign banker who declined to be named said the trend would be long lasting only if Turkey signals that it is determined to take tough structural actions, such as privatisation and improving loss-making pension funds.
The Turkish parliament reopened earlier this week after a two-month summer recess.

It will start to debate a series of key draft laws after mid-October, including the 1997 budget law, corruption probes against Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, emergency rule in the southeast and the extension of a mandate for a Western air force patrolling northern Iraq.
The opposition parties are expected to speed up and toughen efforts to overthrow Erbakan's coalition government.
The parties say the economy is performing badly and the democratic and secular regime is remained under threat.
Economists and brokers do not see two economic resource packages, unveiled by the goverment, as serious measures to rescue the inflation-riddled economy.

Kursat Oral, assistant to general manager of Meksa securities said: "There is a short period in which we don't expect any major economic problem. But I do not have any idea for the mid- and long-term."
